title: How Failure Can Be Good For Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that shielding students from failure through endless do-overs, extended deadlines, and grading curves does more harm than good. He contends that failure teaches lessons success cannot — revealing carelessness, humbling students, and motivating genuine effort — and that denying students the "plain, hard truth" that they fell short removes the intrinsic motivation to improve. While acknowledging that success looks different across grade levels and that students must first be set up for success through clear objectives and adequate teaching, he insists that once that groundwork is laid, teachers should let final, unaltered consequences stand for substandard work or effort. He frames the willingness to let failure be final as an act of integrity that respects students enough to tell them the truth, contrasting it with the "unreliable feedback" that comes from artificially propping up every student's results. The piece closes by tying occasional, well-earned failure to building a tenaciously motivated class.
points: Shielding students from failure through do-overs and grade inflation removes the intrinsic motivation to improve.
Denying students the plain truth that they fell short gives them unreliable feedback about their actual performance.
Teachers must first set students up for success — clear objectives, modeling, and practice — before assigning graded work.
Once expectations are properly taught, consequences for poor effort or sub-par work should be final, with no second chances on that assignment.
Allowing well-earned failure, within a system that gives every student a real chance to succeed, builds a more motivated class.
quotes: Failure teaches us more than our successes. It reveals our mistakes and areas needing improvement.
Rarely are they required to face the plain, hard truth that they fell short.
When you give chance after chance after chance, happily accepting just about anything and everything, no matter how below par, you remove the intrinsic motivation to do better next time.
This underscores the critical importance of setting your students up for success before assigning graded work.

And if they don’t, if they choose to give a poor effort, if they turn in sub-par work or complete a test without care, if they don’t meet the standard you’ve set for them, then give them exactly what they’ve earned.
Stick to your guns. Be a teacher of integrity. Allow your students to learn the hard but life-changing lessons now, when they still have time.
As long as you provide every student the opportunity to succeed, the prospect of failure is one of the keys to creating a tenaciously motivated class.
